p01.why: The block declaration makes the hidden friend visible in read, so the call finds it.

p02.why: The using-declaration makes x private in D, so d.x outside D is rejected; EDG 7.0 accepts it because x is public in B (Q-0052).

p03.why: A non-member cannot use a protected member.

p04.why: A public member of a public base stays public.

p05.why: Overload resolution picks the private put(int) for an int argument, and the public put(long) does not rescue the call.

p06.why: Inspector is a friend class, so its member can read secret.

p07.why: D forms the pointer to the protected member with D, as &D::x.

p08.why: The unqualified name A in D refers to the injected name of B's private base, which D cannot access.

p09.why: A class derived from a friend gets no access.

p10.why: Argument-dependent lookup finds the hidden friend through the target argument.

p11.why: A local class in a member function has that function's access.

p12.why: The deduced type is never named, and v is a public member of Hidden.

p13.why: A non-member names a private static member.

p14.why: The destructor is protected, so f cannot declare a local B.

p15.why: A friend of a friend gets no access.

p16.why: The friend is declared in the namespace, and argument-dependent lookup finds it as well.

p17.why: The using-declaration names a private base member that D cannot access.

p18.why: Argument-dependent lookup finds the hidden friend, which can read x.

p19.why: Union members are public by default.

p20.why: The target type selects the private f(int), and both the member and the friend have access.

p21.why: The unqualified name A in C refers to the injected name of B's private base.

p23.why: After the namespace declaration, ordinary lookup finds the friend.

p24.why: The using-declaration under public raises x to public in D.

p25.why: D uses the protected member through itself and through a D object.

p26.why: D uses a protected member through a B object, which is not a D.

p27.why: A static protected member has no limit on the object class.

p28.why: The block declaration ends with its block, and the call has no argument for argument-dependent lookup.

p29.why: class makes B a private base, so the conversion outside D is not valid.

p30.why: C needs access to the private Other::hidden to befriend it.

p31.why: A member function can use the private members of another object of its class.

p32.why: A public member of a protected base is protected in D, and D can use it.

p33.why: reveal is a friend and is declared in the namespace.

p34.why: Lookup finds D::f, which hides B::f and is private.

p35.why: Ordinary lookup does not find the hidden friend and the call has no arguments.

p38.why: A nested class has access to the enclosing class's private members.

p39.why: The instantiation for int picks the private f(int), checked in the template.

p41.why: The public path through B gives the most access, so x is public in D.

p42.why: Overload resolution picks the private f(int).

p43.why: A class can have any labels in any order.

p44.why: The qualified name ::A names the class through its namespace.

p45.why: Hidden is a private member type named outside the class.

p46.why: Only Reader::read is a friend, so Reader::other cannot read secret.

p47.why: The namespace declaration makes qualified lookup find the friend.

p48.why: The default argument is checked at the declaration, inside the class.

p49.why: The return type of a member definition outside the class has a member's access.

p50.why: a is public and get is public.

p53.why: An access label has no effect on a friend declaration.
